articles.title: 2016: a year in photographs
articles.summary: It’s been emotional
articles.body_text: “May you live in interesting times” is a famous curse. We may disagree on whether 2016 was a good year or if it deserves to be cast into the garbage fires of history, but at the very least we can’t deny that it was interesting. The photos that we took over this last year only prove that point. We photographed an incredible array of subjects: from Michelle Obama to the director of Warcraft; from the best live music performances of Panorama to the classic performance cars of the Goodwood Festival of Speed; from tiny lizards to small dogs to Hollywood legends, we shot them all. And of course, we captured umpteen pictures of every conceivable gadget under the sun. We also got really good at arranging things neatly. The following collection of photographs have not been selected because they’re necessarily the best of the year, but because they’re our favorites. We have edited out a number of great pictures — including many taken by some of the talented freelance photographers who have worked for us this year. Instead, we chose to focus on those pictures that mean the most to us, for whatever reason. We’d love to hear from you about those pictures you think we should have included. Trust me, we’re still arguing about that ourselves. —James Bareham The photographs below are arranged chronologically by the date they were first published. JANUARY [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723629/akrales_160108_0928_A_0133_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Neon Boneyard The Verge team spends much of CES trapped inside the Las Vegas Convention Center. But to test out Polaroids Snap camera, I sought out relics of old Las Vegas. The entrance to the Neon Museum’s Boneyard is a 1960’s sign from Jerry’s Nugget casino, which looked amazing against a post-sunset sky. —Amelia Holowaty Krales FEBRUARY [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723617/akrales_160203_0927_A_1772_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Laura Poitras Laura Poitras is best known for her documentary, Citizenfour about the classified documents she received from Edward Snowden. Visitors to her show Astro Noise at the Whitney Museum were able to view those documents; interact with surveillance technology; and watch interrogation and drone video feeds in the most intimate ways, like these wall cut-outs in a pitch black room. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723651/akrales_160502_1038_B_0070_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Manus X Machina at the Met Manus X Machina, held at the Fashion Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, was a huge exhibition showcasing the intersection of fashion and technology. Everything from incredibly intricate embroidery to 3D-printed dresses were on display. It was an amazing collection of wearable art. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723623/jbareham_160212_0941_0053_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Nextbit Robin The Nextbit Robin wasn’t only the first review I shot after joining The Verge. It was also the first time I combined my passions for Knolling — arranging things really neatly — and sketching into one single photograph. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723637/samsung-galaxy-mwc-2016-251.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Samsung MWC I knew from the beginning of Samsung’s Mobile World Congress press event that they were going to want everyone in the audience to wear the VR headsets that had been placed under their seats. So when the time came, I stood up and shot as much and as fast as I could. It’s not often you get a chance to shoot a room full of a few thousand people all wearing VR headsets — though I was so focused on getting my shot that I totally missed Zuck coming down the aisle across the room. I don’t think I could have gotten in position quickly enough to have captured this dystopian photo of the Facebook CEO we all now know and love, but it would’ve been close. —Sean O’Kane [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723725/vsavov_1346_lamborghini_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Sick Lambo One of more than 400 photos I shot of an ultra exclusive Lamborghini Centenario. The irony of it was that each of the 40 examples of this car that were produced had already been sold by the time of the Geneva Motor Show 2016. So, all we could really do was soak in the sights, emotionally and digitally. —Vlad Savov MARCH [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723621/jbareham_160114_0931_0153_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] FLOTUS Photographing Michelle Obama at the White House is not only a highlight of this year, it is one of the highlights of my entire career. The first lady was gracious, charming, patient, trusting, and, most importantly, completely at ease with my direction. And she never once seem annoyed by me constantly shouting “Fantastic!” This is my favorite photo from the entire session because it shows that we did actually take our own Verge orange seamless backdrop to the White House. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723619/jbareham_160310_0958_0131_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Avegant Glyph The Avegant Glyph was a fairly nondescript piece of technology that seemed to pose more questions than it answered. But what it did do very well was shine bright light into Dieter’s pale blue eyes and make him look like a White Walker from Game of Thrones. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723643/akrales_160319_0972_C_0047.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] SXSW On the Street On the last night of SXSW, Jamieson Cox and I decided we wanted to make a portrait of the event. So we set up a mini studio on 6th Street — one of the main arteries of Austin — that had been closed off for the event. It was packed with people, and music poured out of bars and venues that lined the street. As soon as we saw Billboard Goldie’s mohawk we just had to stop her and take her picture. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723631/jbareham_160329_1003_0050_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] iPad Pro 9.7 One of the key features of the iPad Pro 9.7 is the “True Tone” screen. It automatically adjusts the tone of the screen (making it either warmer or cooler) to compensate for the color temperature of the surrounding ambient light. This feature also proved to be an ideal visual theme for the product shoot, as well as a cool (pun intended) way of differentiating this model of iPad from the many that have gone before. —James Bareham APRIL [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723641/jbareham_160322_0986_0023_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Ford CEO When Ford CEO Mark Fields was in the city to attend the New York Motor Show, he told us he would be more than happy to drop by for a chat and photo shoot. After wracking my brain to think of a suitable backdrop for the portraits, it suddenly dawned upon me that as Mark Fields was making the effort to come by The Verge office, I should photograph him in The Verge office. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723645/akrales_160406_1005_A_018.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] LG-G5 The defining design element of the LG G5 is its modular parts. After some brainstorming with the editorial and video teams, we decided the best way to illustrate the idea was the most modular toy in the world: Lego! I spent more time arranging the Lego around the phone and its various attachments than I care to remember; even “scattering” the Lego to the edge of the frame took ages. Taking the shot itself took a fraction of the time! —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723633/jbareham_160412_0999_A_0033_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] HTC 10 The most striking feature of the HTC 10 is the beautifully designed aluminum body. So I decided to use the removable side from an old Mac Pro as the background and decorated it with various memory modules from the Mac arranged very neatly. Amelia used the same electronic elements in her detail shots. We both wondered how long it would take someone to identify the parts once the HTC 10 review went live. The answer was about six minutes. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723639/20160205-LIM-Innovations-438_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Prosthetic Limbs One of the first features I shot after joining The Verge was about the technological advances in medicine, specifically adjustable and modular prosthetic sockets. We met Robert Spotswood, a car accident survivor who lost his right leg in the crash. With this new adjustable socket, he can play sports for an extended period of time. We spent a few days with him as he went rock climbing and golfing in San Francisco’s Presidio. I was hoping to get an outdoors portrait of Robert that day, but the sun was just way too bright, so I had to look for the next best thing. —Vjeran Pavic [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723625/jbareham_160418_0931_0086_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Launch of Circuit Breaker The launch of Circuit Breaker, “The World’s Greatest Gadget Blog,” was an important milestone for The Verge in 2016. As Circuit Breaker is all about gadgets, the only logical creative direction for the lead image was to take a shot of as many gadgets as we could possibly find. I think that we emptied our entire reviews closet in the making of this photograph. —James Bareham MAY [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723661/akrales_160428_1031_A_0210.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] IMAX Spin Class Though Dami Lee reported this IMAX spin class was less than exciting, I left the shoot with this picture, which made the day a huge success in my book. And as James commented, “There is literally no caption that can do this photo justice. Just know that this man is out there being awesome.” —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723649/jbareham_160511_1049_0319_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Dodge Viper We spent a sunny day at the Monticello Motor Club in New York filming Jason Harper driving a violently yellow Dodge Viper at great speed. I had two principle roles that day: to drive the minivan video chase car as smoothly as possible without crashing, and secondly, to take a turn in the back of the van to shoot some stills. Shooting out of moving vehicle wearing a harness is always fun. I leaned out as far and as low as I could to shoot the Viper on a wide angle lens (which meant it had to get close) and used the slowest shutter speed possible to blur the track but keep the car sharp. — James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723663/akrales_160513_0994_FIN_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Meal Delivery Kaitlyn Tiffany had decided to review a number of different “ready-to-make” meals that were shipped directly to her. For about a month, I photographed her making (and eating) those meals. But we needed a single image that could sum up the whole experience, and the suggestion was to create a scene of “kitchen chaos.” So I dragged almost the entire contents of my kitchen into the studio — there was literally not a single frying pan or spatula left behind. Even my pot rack was rigged up to the ceiling. All that was missing were a few colleagues to throw flour and peas in the air on cue.—Amelia Holowaty Krales JUNE [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723721/vrg_1066_goPro_05_1500_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] GoPro For Sean O’Kane’s in-depth feature on GoPro, I wanted to deconstruct their iconic camera and shoot the different stages of disassembly all the way down to the bare chassis. As we were preparing the shoot, features editor Michael Zelenko posed the question: “Can we also cut it half?” The answer was of course yes. All we needed was a water-jet saw. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7725127/sokane_160523_1066_7445_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] GoPro CEO GoPro CEO Nick Woodman is a charmer. But he’s also the head of a big company that just went through its most troubling year. GoPro’s success is all about Woodman going forward. Its future depends on his ability to sooth the worries of investors, and the success (or failure) of his biggest bets, like the Karma drone. It’s hard to capture a portrait that reflects all that in the waning minutes of an hour-long interview, so I just went straightforward with it, snapping a few photos of the man in his office — the place where he calls those shots. —Sean O’Kane [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723655/jbareham_160523_1065_0067_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Duncan Jones and Warcraft The interior design of Bowery Hotel in New York’s Lower East Side can best be described as a fusion of Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, which basically meant it was the perfect location to shoot the very charming, surprisingly relaxed Duncan Jones, director of the film Warcraft. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723685/acura-nsx-supercar-3037_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Acura NSX I have plenty of shots from our Acura NSX shoot of the car in motion, but my favorite part about that day was dropping the $160,000 supercar in the middle of a tiny town along the Connecticut / New York border. We parked it in front of a diner for some beauty shots and watched patrons ogle it mid-bite, food practically falling from their mouths. The thing was, between shots, we were drooling, too. —Sean O’Kane [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723723/jbareham_160607_0938_0022_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] E-Waste The lead image for our e-waste feature turned into one of the most unexpected creative highlights of 2016. The idea was fairly simple: make a real model of the New York subway map out of some of the actual e-waste this city recycles by the ton on a daily basis. All we needed was a water-jet saw we’d used to slice the GoPro, some wood, and a lot of patience. After weeks of work researching and building the model, taking the pictures took about 10 minutes. You can read more about the making of this photo here. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723671/akrales_160607_1076_A_0227.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Aquaponics When I heard about an indoor aquaponic farm that grows basil in water and is fertilized with the poop of Tilapia fish, I had to check it out. Alessandra Potenza and I visited Verticulture Farms at the top floor of the former Pfizer building in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn. It was fascinating to see how the system works. Verticulture and other outfits like it are hoping to redefine the concept of “local” produce. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723717/jbareham_160625_1070_C_0034_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The Goodwood Hill in a Ferrari This summer I returned to the Goodwood Festival of Speed for the first time in over 15 years. I interviewed the founder of the event, Lord Charles March, and I strolled through the paddocks marveling at eclectic collection of cars dating from the earliest years of the 20th century to the present day. But the highlight by far was a riding up the famous hill in a Ferrari 488 GTB driven by one of Ferrari’s chief instructors. The hill was treacherous, wet from days of rain, muddy in places. As we approached the start line — passing by a long line of some of the most exotic cars in the world, including the new Bugatti Chiron, a very rare Ferrari FXX-K, and an even rarer Aston Martin Vulcan — the sun briefly peered through the clouds. It glinted off the soaking road as we approached the start line. With the unmistakable howl of the 660 hp V8, we launched toward the first corner. The deft confidence of the driver was extraordinary. The Ferrari twitched in that first slippery, tight turn but he compensated instantly, adjusting the suspension settings as we went. His light, gentle touch on the steering wheel starkly contrasted the violence of acceleration, late breaking and staggering amounts of grip. At one stage, we passed so close to some of the treacherous flint walls on the hill that I thought we’d lose the wing mirror. My driver drove so fast we caught the car that had started ahead of us, forcing us to slow down and practically coast across the finish line. The drive was over in just a few minutes. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723681/vsavov_1346_7306.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The Classic Cars of Goodwood Being a Serious Journalist, I had an early morning meeting on my first day at Goodwood. But my route there delayed me greatly, as it was through a paddock of utterly gorgeous retro and modern racing cars, all in operational condition. Smartphone photos snatched en route turned into a vast gallery with my pro camera. Practically impossible to pick a favorite from the bunch, and the experience of walking through the exhibition area was a visual feast worthy of attending the Goodwood Festival of Speed just on its lonesome. —Vlad Savov [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723667/akrales_160707_1084_A_0252.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Visceral Recess by Future Wife Summer of 2016 marked the first ever Panorama Music Festival co-presented by The Verge. The three-day event on Randall’s Island also hosted The Lab, a tech / art exhibit located on the festival grounds. In the months leading up to the event we visited each of the selected artists in their studios to see their works in progress. Beau Burroughs is the creative mind behind Future Wife and interactive work Visceral Recess, a sort of adult bouncy castle with a modern design sensibility. The structure was outfitted with sensors that, when triggered by movement, changed the colored lights that were strung inside it. I was at least eight months pregnant at the time and can vouch for how comfortable it was. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723679/akrales_160531_1075_A_0283_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Gabriel Pulecio Brooklyn-based artist Gabriel Pulecio was the first of the Panorama artists we visited to check out his work, Infinite Wall — a piece you have to experience to feel its full effect. We documented the space and the prototype; the full-size piece was about to be fabricated. The combination of responsive LED lights and mirror panels were exciting to see and provided a taste of what he would present at The Lab at Panorama. —Amelia Holowaty Krales JULY [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723669/vrg_1103_thevoid_lead_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Ghostbusters VR I photographed senior reporter Adi Robertson and business editor Ben Popper decked-out with headsets, backpacks, and “blasters” moments before they entered The Void’s Ghostbusters experience at Madame Tussaud’s in Times Square. The ghosts were successfully vanquished. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723675/vrg_1081_grid_02_fin_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Iris Scans To illustrate a story about the FBI collecting iris scans, I wrangled a bunch of co-workers to sit for a brief, though slightly painful portraits of their eyes. Using a ring light strobe (you can see the lights reflection) and a macro lens I got as close as possible. The individual photos were then composited together into this single image. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723673/akrales_160711_1120_A_0585.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Manhattanhenge The thing about getting a photo of “Manhattanhenge” is positioning: you need a good spot. Alessandra Potenza and I left the office to watch the sunset line up perfectly between the buildings along a street that runs east to west of Manhattan. We chose 42nd street because of a raised roadway by Grand Central station where we could get a full view of the sunset and be safely above the congestion of cars and people below. Even though the road is strictly for vehicles, we were not the first ones there on foot. Even at 5PM we struggled to find a spot for the sunset happening about two hours later. To make matters worse, a police officer soon dispersed the group. Undeterred, we walked further east and joined a crowd that had taken over the street, stopping at each red light to capture the scene, phones in the air. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723705/cwelch_160720_1145_0004_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Moto Z I was having trouble shooting a keeper main image for the Moto Z review, and late into the night at The Verge’s NYC office, this is what I settled on: putting the phone and MotoMods on a green couch and snapping a shot from above. The green fabric worked well for Android. Sometimes simplicity wins. —Chris Welch [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723693/jbareham_160723_1129_0226_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Panorama: Kendrick Lamar Kendrick Lamar was one of the headline acts at this year’s Panorama festival. When it became clear that it was going to be impossible to get near the stage to photograph his set, I decided to go into the crowd to shoot their view of his show instead. At one point Kendrick asked the crowd to turn on the flashes and hold their phones aloft. They instantly obeyed. This photo summed up the entire festival for me. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723677/panorama-finals-0862_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Panorama: Grace Potter I could (and have) spent hours combing through the photos I took at Panorama, but this was one of my favorite moments of one of my favorite sets. This is Grace Potter putting everything she had into a mid-day set like it was a headlining slot at Reading and Leads. We’ve reached a total saturation point when it comes to music festivals, but that doesn’t mean you can’t find wonderful moments from killer artists like Potter. —Sean O’Kane [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723665/MP_herzog-5304_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Werner Herzog This wonderful portrait of Werner Herzog was shot for The Verge by Mike Piscitelli — the only freelance photographer whose work we have included in this review. Mike’s photograph beautifully captures this famous and enigmatic director, whose question about Pokémon Go became one of the best quotes of the year: “When two persons in search of a pokémon clash at the corner of Sunset and San Vicente is there violence? Is there murder?” —James Bareham AUGUST [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723657/jbareham_160526_1073_0011_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Scott Kelly This is a portrait of the astronaut Scott Kelly on the deck of the USS Intrepid, standing in front of a WWII fighter. There’s literally nothing more to add. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723691/jbareham_160811_1180_B_0084_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Galaxy Note 7 Taking photos for The Verge’s review of the Galaxy Note 7 was in itself uneventful. But looking back, this shot of the Samsung’s infamous premier phablet lying upside down in a pool of water like a drowned corpse became vaguely prophetic. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723719/vlad_zero_01_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Hero Headphones This was my first attempt at creating a conceptual image for a review — something more than just a neatly arranged photograph. The original shot didn’t have a perfect circle, the white paper surrounding the red was distinctly gray and crinkled, and the desired effect was not evident. But then Photoshop came to the rescue, salvaging reality with a pleasing dose of fabricated clarity and precision. —Vlad Savov [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723687/jbareham_160802_1169_B_0008_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Nerf Gun For some reason, I just really like this shot of a nerf gun taken for our “Back to School” gift guide. It’s just so bold, bright, colorful and well... Nerf-y. —James Bareham SEPTEMBER [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723689/jbareham_160910_1215_C_0102_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] iPhone 7 The review of the iPhone 7 was, without a doubt, the hardest shoot of the year. First of all, it’s the new iPhone, so it had to be really good. Second, the turn-around time between getting our hands on the new phone and the embargoed publish date was just four days during which Nilay had to review the phone and we had to shoot both stills and video — then edit, retouch, and publish. To top it all I decided, for some inexplicable reason, to surround the iPhone with 25 lenses, each of which had to have all the dust and awkward reflections cleaned up in Photoshop. I spent over seven hours retouching the final set of images. But I like to think that it was worth it. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7724113/vpavic_160712_1138_0079_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Facebook Data Center One of my favorite trips this year was to Prineville, Oregon. Home to about 9,000 people it’s also where you can find many tech giants’ data centers — including Facebook. Getting this shot was a bit more challenging than it might seem. There were a lot of people on the tour, so getting a photo without anyone else in it was tricky. Added to that, the room was very dark and I really wanted to keep everything in focus, so a tripod was a must. We also had three more buildings to go see, so I had to move fast. —Vjeran Pavic [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723713/tconnors_160824_1227_1992_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Robot Wars I consider myself a piss-poor photographer, and can’t for the life of me keep straight the difference between aperture, ISO, and f-stop. But I knew that The Verge’s first trip to China would provide some amazing opportunities to capture things we had never seen before. So I brought along a camera. This shot was taken the morning before the launch of DJI’s Robomasters competition. The stadium was empty and the battlefield wasn’t cluttered with dueling robots yet. The production team was testing out lighting effects and graphics packages for the big screen. It was a still moment just before the action commenced, and somehow it captured the epic nature of the tournament that would ensue. —Ben Popper OCTOBER [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723683/jbareham_160930_1240_0017_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Year of VR: Sony PlayStation 2016 has been the year of virtual reality. Few reporters know more about VR than The Verge’s Adi Robertson, and so over the course of this past year, I photographed her wearing a variety of VR headsets: the Oculus Rift; the HTC Vive; Playstation VR; and the Google Daydream. Playstation VR was unique amongst the four as it was the only headset that provided its own lighting. Very Stranger Things. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723697/vpavic_150816_1187_0287_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] BMW Art Cars I’m not much of a car person, I have never cared too much about driving or even shooting them. There are only a few cars I find truly beautiful on today’s market. But once you stand in front of BMW’s Art Cars, you just can’t help but feel inspired. Pictured above is the 1975 BMW CSL, designed by Alexander Calder. —Vjeran Pavic [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723703/sokane_161013_1246_0009_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Google Pixel I don’t shoot too many produced lead images — that’s why we hired James, after all, and his work speaks for itself in this piece. But I knew right away that I wanted to create something familiar when I got the call to shoot the Pixel review. We planned to set it in a diner, but had to fake our way with a bar instead. I think it was important that the lead (and the rest of the shoot) help echo that familiar tone, because Google’s “first” phone feels like it’s been around for years. —Sean O’Kane NOVEMBER [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723701/vrg_1229_mckesson_profile_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] DeRay McKesson It took almost a month and over 20,000 air miles flying between the East and West Coasts of the US to photograph the nine portraits for Verge 2021. So it’s somewhat ironic that one of my favorites from the entire series was shot in our own Verge studio. DeRay McKesson’s genuine optimism was nothing short of inspiring. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723711/akrales_161026_1250_0004.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] DJI Mavic There was lots of drone news this year, and I am not a drone expert, but there’s something about the design of this little device that I love. Mostly because when you fold up it’s arms it looks like a dead bug. —Amelia Holowaty Krales [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723709/jbareham_161108_1263_0066_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] MacBook Pro Touch Bar For our initial review of the new 13-inch MacBook Pro, Vjeran Pavic photographed a top-down shot of Vlad Savov using the laptop to edit a photograph in Photoshop. When it came to shooting the 13-inch Macbook Pro with the added Touch Bar, I attempted to shoot the most meta photograph possible by featuring both laptops in one single image. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723727/akrales_161116_1281_A_0314.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Snapchat Spectacles Everyone in the office was very excited about the Snapchat Spectacles so it was fun when I finally got to see them up close when I photographed Sean O’Kane for his review. The theme was spending a day out and about snapping videos in different situations. This whimsical image was my favorite from the shoot: we were up on the High Line (a raised former railway turned park on the west side of Manhattan), the leaves were in full of fall color and I noticed how the yellow details on the glasses matched the broad leaves of the trees lining the walkway. —Amelia Holowaty Krales DECEMBER [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723699/tconnors_160523_1301_0026_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Cracking the Elaborate Code This machine isn’t some kind of zened-out space station, nor is it some kind of Seven Days-inspired time machine. It is, however, the first step into a new future for both robotics and virtual reality. In this photograph, projectors lining the top of a geodesic dome are firing out a mapping pattern. This allows the researchers at Carnegie Mellon University to pinpoint the exact location of 500 cameras surrounding The Verge’s business editor Ben Popper. Their goal is to capture 3D models of our body language so that one day they can help endow machines with the capacity to understand the elaborate code of nonverbal communication. —Tom Connors [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723707/jbareham_161207_1305_0125_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] HP Spectre I ended 2016 as I began, combining my love of Knolling and sketching to shoot the most impressive Windows laptop of the year: the HP Spectre x360. Having drawn a detail of the beautifully designed hinge, I arranged the sketchbook, aluminum propelling pencils (one of which I bought years ago from Tokyu Hands in Japan), note pads (with obligatory Verge sticker) and marker pens as neatly as humanly possible. —James Bareham [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7723715/akrales_161216_1331_A_0215_2016.0.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Beats Solo 3 It was a cold day, but I was determined to get out of the office and photograph these Beats headphones in the world where they would mostly be used. I am lucky enough to have co-workers who don’t mind doubling as models so I begged for an hour of Mariya’s time. There is an interesting wall of ivy not far from the office that I had kept in mind for a shoot and I think the texture worked nicely against the fur lining of Mariya’s coat. —Amelia Holowaty Krales Photography by James Bareham, Tom Connors, Amelia Holowaty Krales, Sean O’Kane, Vjeran Pavic, Mike Piscitelli, Ben Popper, Vlad Savov, and Chris Welch. Retouching (from September onwards) by Rosy Warren. Edited by Megan Farokhmanesh, Kaitlyn Tiffany.

articles.title: Snapchat Spectacles are here and they are ridiculously fun
articles.summary: The Verge is about technology and how it makes us feel. Founded in 2011, we offer our audience everything from breaking news to reviews to award-winning features and investigations, on our site, in video, and in podcasts.
articles.body_text: When Snap, Inc. announced earlier this year that it had created a pair of video-recording sunglasses called Spectacles, it was a little hard to get a handle on just what the end result would be. Snap was new to the hardware game, and more ambitious wearables like Google Glass had been expensive, niche failures. But yesterday a limited number of Spectacles went on sale, offered through a yellow pop-up vending machine near the company’s original headquarters in Venice, California — and we finally got a chance to see what the company had come up with. After spending some time with them, I don’t think I’m ever going to give my Spectacles up. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7453019/bbishop_161111_1279_0012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] That vending machine gambit sets up a core ideal — Spectacles are supposed to be whimsical and fun — and that principle carries through all the way to the design and execution of the product. Spectacles are packaged in a clear tube roughly the size of three tennis balls, which holds the recharging case, the glasses themselves, a USB cable for the case, and a glasses cleaning cloth — cut in the shape of the Snapchat ghost. The Spectacles themselves come in three different colors: black, teal, and coral (in person, the coral option looked more like a plain orange, though I ended up with the classic black, myself). Design-wise, they’re plastic glasses that look like a Ray-Ban riff you’d expect Warby Parker to come up with. But pulling them out of the case for the first time, I was pleasantly surprised by just how slim and light they are. They’re not as streamlined as the Wayfarers I personally wear day to day by any means, but the Spectacles keep the bulk of their electronics in the temples of the glasses, letting the rest of the frame and arms feel like, well, just regular sunglasses. Two yellow circles sit at the ends of the glasses: one is where the camera is housed, and the other hides a ring of LEDs that light up when the device is recording.

articles.title: Werner Herzog on the future of film school, critical connectivity, and Pokémon Go
articles.summary: ‘Unfortunately, film school is not going to go extinct. I wish it would.’
articles.body_text: Repetition is a powerful tool for both filmmakers and teachers, and Professor Werner Herzog wants you to know two things: he doesn’t have a cell phone (later he will tell you that he does, but only for emergencies) and he didn’t know movies existed until he was 11. He’s dropped these facts both as humorous anecdotes and boastful claims at screenings of his upcoming documentary Lo and Behold, in the video lectures for his recently released online filmmaking course with MasterClass, and in our conversation two weeks ago in Los Angeles. It’s a provocation of sorts — after all, who would trust a man without a cell phone to direct a documentary about our connected world? Who would trust someone who didn’t grow up dazzled by Star Wars or Spielberg to teach filmmaking?

Apple strikes deal with MLB to provide every team with iPad Pros
articles.summary: Sports announcers are finally allowed to call tablets “iPads”
articles.body_text: Apple and Major League Baseball have signed a multi-year deal that will see every team receive iPad Pro tablets for use in the dugout, reports The Wall Street Journal. The 12.9-inch tablets will be used with rugged, MLB-branded cases based on the one from STM pictured below, and a custom app called MLB Dugout will help managers see performance statistics, check videos from earlier games, and analyze how pitchers and hitters are likely to perform against each other. The deal is reminiscent of the one Microsoft struck with the NFL to have Surface tablets on the sideline of each game, with one difference — iPad use is optional for MLB teams, whereas Surfaces are mandatory in the NFL. MLB teams will get their own personalized data preloaded onto the tablets before each game. Laptops, smartphones, and tablets have long been banned in MLB dugouts, but that ban is being lifted alongside the Apple agreement. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/6262481/dux1_4.0.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “I started in this game 25 years ago and the single biggest change has been the emergence and predominance of analytics,” MLB commissioner Rob Manfred tells the WSJ. “It affects the way we judge players, make decisions on the field and the way fans consume the game.” Apple’s marketing SVP Phil Schiller says “We’re not just replacing binders with tablets, we’re actually helping them do things that weren’t possible before.” Financial details of the deal haven’t been made available.

articles.title: SMHI: Kraftiga regnskurar och risk för översvämningar
articles.summary: SMHI har utfärdat gula varningar för skyfallsliknande regn i delar av södra Sverige under söndagen.
articles.body_text: Under söndagen har SMHI utfärdat gula varningar för skyfallsliknande regn i delar av södra Sverige. – Det kan vara av och till, det kan dyka upp de här kraftigare skurarna ända in på måndagen, säger Sandra Fyrstedt, meteorolog på SMHI. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Under lördagen blev det riktigt besvärligt med översvämningar, bland annat på en camping i Lidköping. Och det ostadiga vädret dröjer sig kvar, framför allt i södra Sverige under söndagen. – Från eftermiddagen och sen vidare också in under måndagen så kan det bli kraftiga skurar över ett område över södra Götaland, säger Sandra Fyrstedt, meteorolog på SMHI . SMHI har utfärdat gula vädervarningar för skyfallsliknande regn i delar av södra Sverige under dagen och fram tills på måndag. I varningsområdena väntas kraftiga regnskurar med en nederbörd på uppemot 40 millimeter. Också åska kan inträffa. – Man får ju tänka på att det då finns risk för översvämningar i samband med de här kraftiga skurarna. Så vet man med sig att man till exempel har en källare som är känslig för kraftigt regn, så kan man ju se över så att vattnet kan ledas bort, säger Sandra Fyrstedt. Hon uppmanar också till eftertänksamhet i trafiken. I norra Sverige ser det ut att vara lugnare väder. – För de som hoppas på sol så kommer man få se den över Norrland på många håll i dag, för där blir det soligt eller växlande molnighet fram på dagen, säger Sandra Fyrstedt. Men så värst värmande kommer inte solen vara. – Det allmänt är svalare väder i hela landet nu. Vi kommer väl som mest upp till 20 grader kanske någonstans i landet, men i allmänhet mellan 14 och 19 grader ligger det på i dag, säger Sandra Fyrstedt.

articles.title: ”Brutal terroristattack”
articles.summary: Ryssland har genomfört den största attacken med ballistiska robotar sedan kriget i Ukraina började, skriver Ukrainas utrikesminister Andrij Sybiha på X. Minst en person har dödats och flera har skadats.
articles.body_text: Ryssland har genomfört den största attacken med ballistiska robotar sedan kriget i Ukraina började, skriver Ukrainas utrikesminister Andrij Sybiha på X. Minst en person har dödats och flera har skadats. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Under natten har Ryssland genomfört ett stort angrepp på Ukraina , främst mot huvudstaden Kiev. ”Ryssland avfyrade det största antalet ballistiska robotar sedan krigets början – omkring fyra dussin – i en brutal terroristattack mot den ukrainska huvudstaden, vilket ledde till att människor dödades och skadades”, skriver utrikesminister Andrij Sybiha på plattformen X. Han uppmanar till ”lämpliga och kraftfulla” svar på attacken, och menar att det behövs läggas ”förödande” press på Ryssland. Ukrainas president Volodymyr Zelenskyj beskriver nattens attacker mot Kiev som ”en av de största attackerna med ballistiska robotar”. Även han ber om omvärldens stöd, och betonar vikten av luftvärnssystem som kan skjuta ner robotar. ”Jag är tacksam för alla som tar våra överenskommelser på allvar och upprätthåller den antiballistiska försvarsförmågan” skriver han på X. Explosioner och flyglarm började höras i Kiev vid 01.30-tiden, skriver Kyiv Independent. Den mest intensiva attackfasen pågick i en dryg timme. Minst en person har dödats i attackerna, och minst 16 har skadats, enligt Zelenskyj. Flera bostadshus, bilar och kontorsbyggnader ska ha träffats, enligt Ukrainas statliga räddningstjänst. Sammanlagt träffade omkring 40 ryska robotar den ukrainska huvudstaden, rapporterar The Guardian. Ryssland ska även ha avfyrat 120 drönare mot Ukraina under natten. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. articles.summary: Österrikiska Salzburg planerar att döpa om gator som fortfarande har namn efter nazister eller personer som gynnades av Hitlerregimen.
articles.body_text: Österrikiska Salzburg planerar att döpa om gator som fortfarande har namn efter nazister eller personer som gynnades av Hitlerregimen. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Att byta ut gatunamn med nazikoppling har dragit ut på tiden i Österrike. I Salzburg beskrevs ett namnbyte i april förra året som ett av de första i sitt slag. I år kommer även Josef Thoraks gata att döpas om till Helene von Taussigs gata, enligt en rapport från kommunen som väntas röstas igenom i stadsfullmäktige. Nästa år ska gatunamnen Hans Pfitzner och Erich Schenk bytas till Anna Reindl och Elsa Bienenfeld. Även gatorna Gustav Resatz och Erich Landgrebe kommer att döpas om. Mer berömda namn får vänta. Herbert von Karajan och Ferdinand Porsche, världskända österrikare som var med i nazistpartiet, nämns i kommunens rapport. Men att stryka deras namn väntas möta mer motstånd. articles.title: Paus för brandmännen i stora brandkatastrofen
articles.summary: Brandmännen i norska Drammen har inte behövt rycka ut under natten till söndagen. Endast bevakningsarbete har pågått – det svala, fuktiga vädret har varit till hjälp.
articles.body_text: Brandmännen i norska Drammen har inte behövt rycka ut under natten till söndagen. Endast bevakningsarbete har pågått – det svala, fuktiga vädret har varit till hjälp. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. – Vi har haft bevakning både i bostadsområdet och i skogen under natten, men från klockan åtta sätts nya brandmän och personal från civilförsvaret in, säger Jan Rundtorn vid norska räddningstjänsten till NTB. Branden har förstört över 100 bostäder och tvingat över 400 personer att evakuera. – Det har regnat en del under natten, med sval och fuktig luft, och det har varit gynnsamt, säger Rundtorn. Polisen uppgav på lördagskvällen att risken för fortsatt spridning av branden har minskat. Det finns fortfarande inga uppgifter om saknade personer. Däremot letar många norrmän fortfarande efter sina husdjur. Frank och Lena Stiby bodde tillsammans med sina två katter i ett av de nedbrunna husen. Katten Leo var hemma och evakuerades tillsammans med paret, men Mio, döpt efter Astrid Lindgrens klassiker ”Mio min Mio”, var utomhus. Med hjälp av gps-sändare kunde paret se att Mio befann sig bland de brandhärjade gatorna, och tillsammans med andra djurägare har de letat efter sina husdjur. På lördagskvällen hittade de till slut sin Mio. – Det är ren lycka. Jag är så lycklig, säger Lena till VG.

articles.title: Unik fågel kan ha häckat i Sverige
articles.summary: Den ringnäbbade måsen är tillbaka på besök i centrala Stockholm, denna gång kanske som förälder. Det rapporterar P4 Stockholm.
articles.body_text: Den ringnäbbade måsen är tillbaka på besök i centrala Stockholm, denna gång kanske som förälder. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. En ringnäbbad mås som hör hemma i Nordamerika kan ha häckat med en fiskmås i Sverige. – För första gången någonsin i Sverige har en ringnäbbad mås häckat och denna gång med en vanlig fiskmås, säger ornitologen Andréas Forsman till radion. Enligt Forsman tyder mycket på att ringmåsen har häckat då den beter sig som en förälder. Men eftersom en tredje fågel har setts vid boet ska en dna-analys fastställa ungarnas härkomst. – Ungarna är ute och flygtränar. Det är väldigt spektakulärt att studera dem på det här sättet, säger Forsman. Han påpekar att man bara en gång tidigare har dokumenterat en ringnäbbad mås som häckat i Europa. Det var i Nordirland 2004. Förra året och tidigare i år syntes den amerikanska måsen i Stockholm. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. articles.title: ALBIN JULIN: Det hon berättar om Abba är helt galet
articles.summary: Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma.
articles.body_text: Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Hur kom det sig att Ruth Kvarnström-Jones, uppväxt i Croft i nordvästra England, började skriva romaner om Stockholm? Scouter från Kristinehamn spelar viss roll, men den utlösande händelsen i kärlekshistorien om Kvarnström-Jones och Sverige stavas Abba. Efter en aha-upplevelse med ”Arrival” gräver hon vidare i Abbornas svenskspråkiga katalog – och en dröm om Stockholm väcks. Abbas helt galna avtryck i det där landet upphör aldrig att förvåna. Ruth Kvarnström-Jones tecknar ett magiskt Stockholmsporträtt. Sommarpromenader genom Kungsträdgården, fester på Alexandras, en Björn Ulvaeus i Stockholm marathon, tv-inspelningen av Clabbe af Geijerstams ”Lite Grand i örat” (en föraning om var hennes uppmärksammade romanserie skulle komma att utspela sig). I Kvarnström-Jones sommarprogram får musiken representera hennes yrke som översättare, bland annat genom Niklas Strömstedts kreativa tolkning av ”Slipping through my fingers”: ”Kan man ha en solkatt i en bur”. Valet känns både smart, effektivt och varmt – precis som sommarpratet i stort. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. Expressen granskar, avslöjar och ger dig senaste nyheterna på ett sakligt sätt. articles.title: Irans svar till Trump: ”Kamikazedrönare”
articles.summary: USA har genomfört en ny våg av luftattacker mot Iran – som i sin tur säger sig ha svarat med ”kamikazedrönare”.
articles.body_text: USA har genomfört en ny våg av luftattacker mot Iran – som i sin tur säger sig ha svarat med ”kamikazedrönare”. Länderna har nu riktat anfall mot varandra under åtta nätter i rad. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. ”Angreppen syftar till att ytterligare försvaga Irans förmåga att hota den kommersiella sjöfarten i Hormuzsundet och att snabbt straffa de styrkor inom Revolutionsgardet som i går kväll genomförde attacker mot amerikanska soldater i Jordanien”, skrev det amerikanska militärkommandot Centcom på X strax efter midnatt. Tidigare i helgen gick USA ut med att två amerikanska soldater hade dödats – de första sedan stridigheterna återupptogs den 7 juli – och att en tredje amerikan saknades efter ”iranska robot- och drönarattacker” mot Jordanien. De iranska regimkopplade nyhetsbyråerna Fars och Tasnim rapporterar under natten mot söndagen om amerikanska attacker mot staden Sirik, belägen vid Hormuzsundet i södra Iran. Smällar har även hörts i bland annat Bandar Abbas, en stad som återkommande attackerats den gångna veckan. Strax före klockan 06, svensk tid, meddelade USA:s militär att nattens anfallsvåg var över – och att den anfallit styrkor tillhörande Revolutionsgardet ”som genomförde attacker mot amerikanska soldater i Jordanien”. Iran säger sig – å sin sida – ha riktat attacker mot två amerikanska baser i Kuwait under natten. I ett uttalande i statlig tv uppger militären att den genomfört ”storskaliga attacker med kamikazedrönare mot den amerikanska militärens ammunitionsdepå vid Camp Udairi samt mot Patriot-radarsystemet och luftövervakningsradarn på Ali Al Salem-flygbasen i Kuwait”. Irans högste ledare Mojtaba Khamenei hotade under lördagen med ”oförglömliga attacker” om USA inte upphör med sina återkommande anfall. Han kallade också – via ombud – USA:s president Donald Trumps signatur för ”värdelös”. Några timmar före Khameneis uttalande tillkännagav landets vice utrikesminister Kazem Gharibabadi att Iran inte längre tillämpar det samförståndsavtal som slöts mellan USA och Iran för en månad sedan. Totalt 16 amerikanska soldater har enligt AP mist livet sedan kriget startade i februari. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. Expressen granskar, avslöjar och ger dig senaste nyheterna på ett sakligt sätt. articles.title: Märkliga fyndet – i hyreshuset
articles.summary: Libby och Aubrey Birrell gjorde en märklig upptäckt i deras hyreshus i San Diego. På en av väggarna hängde en bild där hela deras familj fanns med.
articles.body_text: Libby och Aubrey Birrell gjorde en märklig upptäckt i sitt hyreshus i San Diego. På en vägg hängde ett foto där hela deras familj fanns med. – Vi var alla jättechockade, säger Aubrey Birrell till Fox News . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Familjen Birrell från Utah var på semester i San Diego med ungefär 30 släktingar. I ett av husen de hyrt via Airbnb hittade systrarna Libby och Aubrey något minst sagt märkligt. På väggen i vardagsrummet hängde ett stort fotografi från en strand. I fotot fanns hela deras familj med, rapporterar Fox News . – I samma ögonblick som vi såg det fick vi alla att komma fram och titta, och vi var alla i jättechockade, säger Aubrey Birrell och fortsätter: – Första gången vi sov måste jag säga att vi tyckte att det var läskigt. De la upp ett klipp på Tiktok där de berättade om mysteriet. Videon blev snabbt viral. Men de kunde inte förstå hur bilden på dem fanns på värdens vägg. – Visste de att vi skulle komma? Vi kände oss mest förvirrade, det var lite kusligt, men också bara chockerande, säger Aubrey Birrell. De kontaktade hyresvärden för att få ett svar på mysteriet. Han berättade då att inredningsarkitekten som möblerat huset är fotograf och brukar ta flygfoton över stränder för att sedan förstora dem som konstverk.

articles.title: Putins drag efter stora bakslagen
articles.summary: Putins skuggflotta beskrivs som avgörande i att finansiera kriget. Att flera av fartygen attackerats har blivit en hård smäll – nu agerar Ryssland.
articles.body_text: Putins skuggflotta beskrivs som avgörande i att finansiera kriget. Att flera av fartygen attackerats har blivit en hård smäll – nu agerar Ryssland. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Ukraina har slagit hårt mot Putins skuggflotta i Svarta havet – nu svarar Ryssland genom att flytta delar av sin mest effektiva drönarenhet, ”Rubicon”. Enligt ukrainska uppgifter ska 200 drönargrupper skydda fartygen. Samtidigt pressas flottan också i Östersjön. Ryska försvarsmakten kommer att förflytta delar av sina drönarenheter för att skydda fartygen i Vladimir Putins skuggflotta. Det uppger den ukrainska befälhavaren för militärgrenen för obemannade styrkor, Robert Brovdi. I skuggflottan ingår fraktfartyg som kringgår sanktionerna mot Ryssland för att kunna transportera olja ut i världen. Inkomsten för den ryska oljan har flera gånger beskrivits som avgörande för att de ska kunna fortsätta bedriva kriget i Ukraina. Men i början av juli inledde Ukraina en ny militäroperation riktad mot just skuggflottan, skriver Kyiv Independent . Försvarsmakten kallade insatsen ”Moskva kommer att falla på grund av Krim”. Under 13 dagar attackerades 172 fartyg i Svarta havet. Utöver tankfartyg anföll man även bogserbåtar, flytande kranar och andra fartyg som Ryssland använder i sina infrastrukturbyggen runt Krimhalvön. Det senaste dygnet attackerades ytterligare 13 fartyg. Nu svarar Ryssland genom att skicka 200 drönargrupper från sin så kallade ”Rubicon”-enhet. Den beskrivs som den mest effektiva drönarenheten inom den ryska militären. Varje enskilt ryskt fartyg kommer att få en egen grupp som försvarar det, enligt befälhavaren Brovdi. Drönargrupperna kommer bara att skickas till Svarta havet och Azovskasjön (vattenkroppen mellan Ryssland, Ukraina och Krimhalvön). Rubicon-enheten kommer i samband med den nya insatsen att delvis dras tillbaka från fronten.

articles.title: Expressen Direkt
articles.summary: Expressens direkflöde med senaste nyheterna i korthet • Största nyhetshändelserna i Sverige och världen
articles.body_text: En person har hittat en sköldpadda under en traktor i Floda, skriver polisen på sin hemsida. Fyndet gjordes under lördagen. Sköldpaddan är en 15 centimeter lång landsköldpadda och ägaren har inte identifierats. Den är i nuläget lämnad till en organisation som kan ta hand om den, men hanteras av polisen som hittegods. Den som äger sköldpaddan, eller vet vem som gör det, uppmanas höra av sig till 114 14. Över 100 personer saknas sedan en färja kapsejsat utanför Guyanas kust i norra Sydamerika. Enligt medier var färjan Barima på väg nordvästerut längs kusten, men skickade ut ett anrop om sjönöd sent på lördagskvällen lokal tid. Några timmar senare ska man ha lyckats rädda ett mindre antal av de 116 personer som befann sig ombord. Branden i Drammen är inte under kontroll, meddelar den norska polisen på söndagsförmiddagen. De uppger att räddningstjänsten har god överblick och att det inte finns någon spridningsrisk, men eftersom det fortfarande är så pass varmt blossar mindre bränder upp. ” Den samlade bedömningen är att branden fortfarande inte är under kontroll ”, skriver polisen. Sex brandhelikoptrar och personal från räddningstjänsten och civilförsvaret deltar fortfarande i insatsen. Polisen i Uppsala fick imorse in samtal om att att djur hade övergivits utanför ett hunddagis i staden. Det visade sig inte handla om hundar – utan om två hönor, som lämnats vid ingången med en kartong och en vattenskål. Polisen åkte dit för att ta hand om hönsen, men man tvingades jaga efter dem ett tag innan man lyckades få fatt i dem. Nu är hönorna tillfälligt inkvarterade hos en veterinär i väntan på ett mer permanent boende.
